question:
Client: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi. Matter: motor accident claim, death of spouse.

Her husband was killed in a road accident involving a commercial truck. The truck driver was operating the vehicle without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies the claim, arguing the policy is void because the driver was unlicensed, and that it bears no liability.

Key facts: deceased aged 42; monthly income Rs 35,000; dependants are the wife and two minor children (8 and 12); the truck was a commercial vehicle owned by a transport company; the driver held no valid licence; the insurer contests liability.

Research the corpus and advise on supporting precedents, adverse precedents, and strategy.

payload.holding: The Supreme Court held that an insurer cannot disown its liability to third parties on the ground that the driver, while possessing a valid light motor vehicle licence, lacked an endorsement to drive the vehicle as a commercial vehicle.
payload.ratio: An insurer cannot avoid its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties under Section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement on their licence to drive it as a commercial vehicle.

17. The heading “Insurance of Motor Vehicles against Third Party Risks” given in Chapter XI of the
Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (Chapter VIII of 1939 Act) itself shows the intention of the legislature to
make third party insurance compulsory and to ensure that the victims of accident arising out of use
of motor vehicles would be able to get compensation for the death or injuries suffered. The provision
has been inserted in order to protect the persons travelling in vehicles or using the road from the
risk attendant upon the user of the motor vehicles on the road. To overcome this ugly situation, the
legislature has made it obligatory that no motor vehicle shall be used unless a third party insurance
is in force.
18. Reading the provisions of Sections 146 and 147 of the Motor Vehicles Act, it is evidently clear
that in certain circumstances the insurer’s right is safeguarded but in any event the insurer has to
pay compensation when a valid certificate of insurance is issued notwithstanding the fact that the
insurer may proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount. Under Section 149 of the Motor
Vehicles Act, the insurer can defend the action inter alia on the grounds, namely, (i) the vehicle was
not driven by a named person, (ii) it was being driven by a person who was not having a duly
granted licence, and (iii) person driving the vehicle was disqualified to hold and obtain a driving
licence. Hence, in our considered opinion, the insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that
although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light
motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was
obtained in the driving licence. In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the
amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer.

21. A reading of the proviso to sub-section (4) as well as the language employed in
sub-section (5) would indicate that they are intended to safeguard the interest of an
insurer who otherwise has no liability to pay any amount to the insured but for the
provisions contained in Chapter XI of the Act. This means, the insurer has to pay to
the third parties only on account of the fact that a policy of insurance has been issued
in respect of the vehicle, but the insurer is entitled to recover any such sum from the
insured if the insurer were not otherwise liable to pay such sum to the insured by
virtue of the conditions of the contract of insurance indicated by the policy.
22. To repeat, the effect of the above provisions is this:
when a valid insurance policy has been issued in respect of a vehicle as evidenced by
a certificate of insurance the burden is on the insurer to pay to the third parties,
whether or not there has been any breach or violation of the policy conditions. But
the amount so paid by the insurer to third parties can be allowed to be recovered
from the insured if as per the policy conditions the insurer had no liability to pay
such sum to the insured.
23. It is advantageous to refer to a two-Judge Bench of this Court in Skandia
Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Kokilaben Chandravadan (1987 )2 SCC 654. Though the said
decision related to the corresponding provisions of the predecessor Act (Motor

Vehicles Act, 1939) the observations made in the judgment are quite germane now as
the corresponding provisions are materially the same as in the Act. Learned Judges
pointed out that the insistence of the legislature that a motor vehicle can be used in a
public place only if that vehicle is covered by a policy of insurance is not for the
purpose of promoting the business of the insurance company but to protect the
members of the community who become sufferers on account of accidents arising
from the use of motor vehicles. It is pointed out in the decision that such protection
would have remained only a paper protection if the compensation awarded by the
courts were not recoverable by the victims (or dependants of the victims) of the
accident.

payload.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
payload.holding: The court held that the insurance companies were jointly and severally liable with the owners to satisfy the third-party claims despite the drivers' licences not being current on the exact date of the accidents, and enhanced the compensation awarded in both claim cases while reducing the interest rate to 9% per annum.
payload.ratio: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party under the Motor Vehicles Act regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence, and the mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence on the date of the accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of its third-party liability.

More often than not, literal interpretation of a statute or a provision of a statute results in absurdity.
Therefore, while interpreting statutory provisions, the Courts should keep in mind the objectives or
purpose for which statute has been enacted. Justice Frankfurter of U.S. Supreme Court in an article
titled as Some Reflections on the Reading of Statutes (47 Columbia Law Reports 527), observed that,
"legislation has an aim, it seeks to obviate some mischief, to supply an adequacy, to effect a change
of policy, to formulate a plan of Government. That aim, that policy is not drawn, like nitrogen, out of
the air; it is evidenced in the language of the statutes, as read in the light of other external
manifestations of purpose".

The inevitable conclusion therefore is that the decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no
application to own damage cases. The effect of fake license has to be considered in the light of what
has been stated by this Court in New India Assurance Co., Shimla v. Kamla and Ors. (2001 (4) SCC
342). Once the license is a fake one the renewal cannot take away the effect of fake license. It was
observed in Kamla's case (supra) as follows:
"12. As a point of law we have no manner of doubt that a fake licence cannot get its
forgery outfit stripped off merely on account of some officer renewing the same with
or without knowing it to be forged. Section 15 of the Act only empowers any Licensing
Authority to "renew a driving licence issued under the provisions of this Act with
effect from the date of its expiry". No Licensing Authority has the power to renew a
fake licence and, therefore, a renewal if at all made cannot transform a fake licence as
genuine. Any counterfeit document showing that it contains a purported order of a
statutory authority would ever remain counterfeit albeit the fact that other persons
including some statutory authorities would have acted on the document unwittingly
on the assumption that it is genuine".
As noted above, the conceptual difference between third party right and own damage cases has to be
kept in view. Initially, the burden is on the insurer to prove that the license was a fake one.

payload.holding: The Court held that where a driving license is renewed more than 30 days after its expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period of the accident, but directed the insurance company to satisfy the award and recover the amount from the insured owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
payload.ratio: When an application for renewal of a driving license is made more than 30 days after its expiry, the license is renewed from the date of renewal; thus, the driver does not hold a valid license on the date of an accident occurring during the lapsed period, absolving the insurer of primary liability, though a 'pay and recover' order may be issued in favour of third-party claimants.

"42. We therefore hold that the multiplier to be used should be as mentioned in
Column (4) of the table above (prepared by applying Susamma Thomas, Trilok
Chandra and Charlie), which starts with an operative multiplier of 18 (for the age
groups of 15 to 20 and 21 to 25 years), reduced by one unit for every five years, that is
M-17 for 26 to 30 years, M-16 for 31 to 35 years, M-15 for 36 to 40 years, M-14 for 41
to 45 years, and M-13 for 46 to 50 years, then reduced by two units for every five
years, that is, M-11 for 51 to 55 years, M-9 for 56 to 60 years, M-7 for 61 to 65 years
and M-5 for 66 to 70 years."
45. In Reshma Kumari, the aforesaid has been approved by stating, thus:-
"It is high time that we move to a standard method of selection of multiplier, income
for future prospects and deduction for personal and living expenses. The courts in
some of the overseas jurisdictions have made this advance. It is for these reasons, we
think we must approve the Table in Sarla Verma for the selection of multiplier in
claim applications made under Section 166 in the cases of death. We do accordingly.
If for the selection of multiplier, Column (4) of the Table in Sarla Verma is followed,
there is no likelihood of the claimants who have chosen to apply under Section 166
being awarded lesser amount on proof of negligence on the part of the driver of the
motor vehicle than those who prefer to apply under Section 163-A.

ation, we are disposed to think when we
accept the principle of standardization, there is really no rationale not to apply the
said principle to the self-employed or a person who is on a fixed salary. To follow the
doctrine of actual income at the time of death and not to add any amount with regard

to future prospects to the income for the purpose of determination of multiplicand
would be unjust. The determination of income while computing compensation has to
include future prospects so that the method will come within the ambit and sweep of
just compensation as postulated under Section 168 of the Act. In case of a deceased
who had held a permanent job with inbuilt grant of annual increment, there is an
acceptable certainty. But to state that the legal representatives of a deceased who was
on a fixed salary would not be entitled to the benefit of future prospects for the
purpose of computation of compensation would be inapposite. It is because the
criterion of distinction between the two in that event would be certainty on the one
hand and staticness on the other. One may perceive that the comparative measure is
certainty on the one hand and uncertainty on the other but such a perception is
fallacious. It is because the price rise does affect a self-employed person; and that
apart there is always an incessant effort to enhance one's income for sustenance. The
purchasing capacity of a salaried person on permanent job when increases because of
grant of increments and pay revision or for some other change in service conditions,
there is always a competing attitude in the private sector to enhance the salary to get
better efficiency from the employees. Similarly, a person who is self-employed is
bound to garner his resources and raise his charges/fees so that he can live with same
facilities. To have the perception that he is likely to remain static and his income to
remain stagnant is contrary to the fundamental concept of human attitude which
always intends to live with dynamism and move and change with the time.

payload.ratio: Where there is consistent and unimpeached oral testimony of an eye-witness establishing the absence of negligence on the part of the deceased, a tribunal cannot record a finding of contributory negligence merely by drawing assumptions from a police sketch or site plan that does not conclusively indicate a head-on collision. Furthermore, even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.

args.question: Motor accident death claim — commercial truck, driver had no valid driving licence, insurer denies liability. Deceased aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, dependants: wife and two minor children (8 and 12).

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to pay third-party compensation under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver lacked a specific endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle. The third party's right to recover from the insurer is statutory and paramount.
supporting.fact_alignment: The case involved a commercial vehicle (Maxi Cab) where the driver held an LMV licence but no commercial endorsement. Our case involves a commercial truck where the driver held no valid licence at all. The principle that third-party rights override policy conditions applies a fortiori.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Supreme Court judgment that directly establishes the primacy of third-party rights over policy breaches. It anchors the argument that National Insurance Co. must pay first and recover later.
supporting.quote: the insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained in the driving licence. In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer's liability to satisfy a third-party award is statutory under Section 149 MV Act. Even if a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence) is proved, the insurer must pay the third party and can recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The case involved a third-party death claim where the driver had an invalid licence. The court held the insurer liable to pay and recover. Directly on point with our facts.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Delhi High Court judgment synthesises the entire line of Supreme Court authority (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the 'pay and recover' principle applies even where the insurer proves a fundamental breach.
supporting.quote: the liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Under Section 149(1) and (4) MV Act, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award as a judgment debtor even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, and is entitled to recover from the insured. This applies irrespective of whether the breach is 'fundamental'.
supporting.fact_alignment: The Full Bench of Karnataka High Court considered the exact defence the insurer will raise — that a fundamental breach (no licence) absolves it. The court held that even fundamental breach does not defeat third-party rights.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest authority against the insurer's 'no liability' argument. It explicitly rejects the argument that a 'fundamental breach' (which driving without any licence would be) allows the insurer to escape third-party liability.
supporting.quote: the insurer or Insurance Company is liable to satisfy the award vis-à-vis a third party and is entitled to recover from the insured. This is irrespective of, the policy being an Act policy... even if there is breach of any condition recognized under Section 149(2), even if it is a fundamental breach.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Even where the insurer proves a fundamental breach (driver had no driving licence at all), the third-party claimant cannot be made to suffer. The insurer must pay the compensation first and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: This is the closest factual match in the corpus: the driver had no driving licence at all (not expired, not wrong class — none). The tribunal still ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This directly refutes the insurer's argument that 'no licence = no liability'. The tribunal held that even a complete absence of a licence is a fundamental breach, but the third party still gets paid.
supporting.quote: the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time... it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1, owner of the offending vehicle.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the required authorisation/badge, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked the proper authorisation for a commercial transport vehicle. Our driver had no licence at all. The principle that breach leads to pay-and-recover, not exoneration, applies.
supporting.why_it_matters: Madras High Court confirms that even where the insurer proves breach, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not avoidance of liability to the third party.
supporting.quote: Keeping in view the nature of injuries... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent - Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV/transport licence but not for a heavy goods vehicle. Our driver had no licence at all. The ratio that third-party rights trump licence defects applies.
supporting.why_it_matters: Madras High Court applies S.Iyyapan and Swaran Singh to confirm that the insurer's remedy is recovery from the owner, not refusal to pay the claimant.
supporting.quote: the insurer cannot disown its liability... In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where there is a breach of policy conditions (lack of special endorsement for hazardous goods), the insurance company cannot escape liability to pay compensation to claimants. Once payment is made, the insurer has the right to recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The breach was a missing special endorsement. Our breach is a missing licence altogether. The principle of pay-and-recover for third-party claims is the same.
supporting.why_it_matters: Punjab & Haryana High Court confirms that even a regulatory breach (special endorsement missing) does not defeat third-party rights — only pay-and-recover follows.
supporting.quote: the insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Even where the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The insurer argued that without a valid licence, it cannot be forced to pay. The court rejected this and ordered pay-and-recover. Directly on point.
supporting.why_it_matters: Allahabad High Court confirms that the 'no valid licence' defence does not allow the insurer to escape third-party liability — only pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: since the valid driving licence of the driver of the Tanker has not been produced, the Insurance Company shall pay the compensation to the claimants and thereafter will have a right to recover it from the owner of the Tanker.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks and has no application to own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that Swaran Singh's liberal approach does not apply where the driver had no licence at all (as opposed to a wrong-class licence). They will argue that 'no licence' is closer to a 'fake licence' situation and that the ratio should be read restrictively.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Laxmi Narain Dhut expressly limits its holding to own-damage claims and disputes between insurer and insured where no third party is involved. Para 3 of the judgment states: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks.' Our case is a third-party death claim, squarely within Swaran Singh's ambit. The judgment actually confirms at point 3: 'In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.' This is a pro-client statement, not adverse.
adverse.quote: The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks... In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
adverse.principle: Where a driving licence has expired and is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, the renewal takes effect from the date of renewal, not retrospectively. The driver does not hold a valid licence on the date of accident.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that a lapsed/no licence is a breach that shifts primary liability to the owner. However, the court still ordered pay-and-recover, so it does not defeat the claim.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports our position: despite finding no valid licence on the accident date, the court directed the insurer to pay the third party and recover from the insured. It is not adverse — it confirms the pay-and-recover principle.
adverse.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence. Non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence does not constitute a fundamental breach.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may argue that this case is about an expired licence (which was later renewed), not a complete absence of a licence, and that a complete absence is a graver breach. However, the case still supports pay-and-recover.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is actually favourable: it holds the insurer liable despite the licence issue. The distinction between 'expired licence' and 'no licence' does not help the insurer because doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket) directly holds that even a complete absence of a licence results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
adverse.quote: the insurance company is bound to satisfy the award passed against the third party and the conditions imposed in the policy would not bind the third party and the amount paid by the insurance company... can be recovered by the insurance company from the insured.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without any licence is a fundamental and statutory breach. The insurer is not directly liable to indemnify the insured, but must pay the third party and recover from the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will rely on the finding that 'no licence' is a fundamental breach and that the insurer is 'absolved from its liability' vis-à-vis the insured. They will argue this supports their position.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The insurer selectively quotes the finding that it is 'absolved from its liability' while ignoring that the tribunal still ordered pay-and-recover. The actual order was: 'direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1, owner of the offending vehicle.' The third party gets paid. This is our case exactly.
adverse.quote: the respondent No.2 insurance company has proved its defense... and as such insurance company is not liable to pay the compensation... But, on the said ground, the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner... it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1.

priority_arguments: Lead with the statutory liability argument under Section 149 MV Act: the insurer's duty to satisfy third-party awards is absolute and independent of policy conditions. Cite S.Iyyapan (doc_032), Satto (doc_033), and Yallavva (doc_025).
Emphasise that the 'pay and recover' principle applies even where the driver had NO licence at all — Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) is the closest factual match and directly on point.

Argue that the insurer's remedy is against the insured owner, not against the third-party claimants. The transport company owner who employed an unlicensed driver bears the ultimate liability, not the widow and children.

On quantum: deceased aged 42, self-employed, monthly income Rs 35,000, 3 dependants. Use Pranay Sethi framework: 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 42), 1/3rd deduction, multiplier 14. Total ~Rs 51 lakhs plus conventional heads (spousal consortium Rs 1.6 lakh, parental consortium for minor children, funeral expenses).
If the insurer argues 'fundamental breach', cite Yallavva (doc_025) Full Bench which holds that even fundamental breach does not defeat third-party rights — only pay-and-recover follows.
If the insurer cites Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031), distinguish it as limited to own-damage claims; the judgment itself confirms that for third-party risks, the insurer must indemnify and recover.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51-53 lakhs) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of claim petition till realisation.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using the Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework. Monthly income Rs 35,000. Age 42 (multiplier 14). Self-employed (25% future prospects per Pranay Sethi for ages 40-50). 3 dependants (1/3rd deduction). Conventional heads: loss of estate Rs 19,965, funeral Rs 19,965, spousal consortium Rs 1,59,720 (Rs 53,240 x 3 for wife and two minor children per Magma General / Satinder Kaur). Total: Rs 50,99,650. If the deceased is found to be in permanent employment (30% future prospects), the figure rises to ~Rs 52.96 lakhs.
risks: The insurer may argue that 'no licence at all' is a graver breach than 'wrong class of licence' and seek to distinguish S.Iyyapan (doc_032). Counter with Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) which directly deals with 'no licence' and still orders pay-and-recover.
The insurer may challenge the income proof (Rs 35,000/month). Ensure robust documentary evidence of income (salary slips, bank statements, IT returns).
The insurer may argue contributory negligence if there is any ambiguity in the accident site plan. Ensure eye-witness testimony is strong and consistent.

The transport company owner may be impleaded and may argue that the insurer should bear full liability. This is not adverse to the claimant — the claimant's position is that either the insurer or the owner pays, and the insurer pays first.

If the insurer delays payment and appeals, the claimants may face delay in realisation. Consider seeking an interim award under Section 140 MV Act (Rs 50,000 on 'no fault' basis) which is payable regardless of the licence defence.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim petition under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Also file a separate application under Section 140 for interim compensation of Rs 50,000 (no-fault liability), which the insurer cannot resist on the ground of licence breach. Seek a declaration that the insurer is liable to pay the entire awarded amount in the first instance with liberty to recover from the insured owner/driver.

caveats: The corpus does not contain the landmark Supreme Court judgments Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297, Pranay Sethi (2017) 16 SCC 680, or Sarla Verma (2009) 6 SCC 121 as separate entries, but these are cited and applied within the corpus judgments. Counsel should have the full texts of these landmark authorities ready.

The corpus contains no judgment where the insurer was completely absolved of third-party liability solely on the ground of an unlicensed driver. The consistent principle across all relevant judgments is pay-and-recover.

If the deceased was in permanent employment (rather than self-employed), the future prospects addition would be 30% instead of 25%, increasing the compensation. Counsel should ascertain the deceased's employment status precisely.

The corpus does not contain any judgment dealing with the specific quantum for a Rs 35,000/month earner at age 42. The quantum computation above is based on the standard Sarla Verma/Pranay Sethi framework as applied in doc_041 and doc_019.

payload.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi
payload.holding: The Court held that while an attached trailer/trolley is part of an insured tractor and does not require separate insurance, the insurance company is absolved from liability because the tractor was being used to transport bricks and iron rods for construction rather than for agricultural purposes, violating the insurance policy terms.
payload.ratio: A trailer attached to a tractor is considered part of the tractor and does not require separate insurance under the Motor Vehicles Act; however, if the tractor is used for non-agricultural purposes in violation of the insurance policy, the insurer is not liable to pay compensation.

passages.text:

On a perusal of the definition of word 'tractor' shows that the tractor itself is not able to carry any

tractor and covered under the insurance policy.
In view of the above, we observed that the trailer/trolley, which is attached with the tractor is a part
of the tractor, which was duly insured from the insurance company. Hence, the insurance company

separately insured.
But in the instant case, fact remains that at the time of accident, the trolley which was attached with

rods and bricks is certainly not an agricultural activity. The tractor was insured only for the purpose
of agricultural activity. The tractor will have to be used only for agricultural purpose not for any
other purpose including the construction of a room. Thus, there is a violation of the terms and
conditions of the insurance policy. When it is so, then we are of the view that in the instant case, the
insurance company is not liable to pay the compensation and the owner of the tractor will have to

supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to pay third-party compensation under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver lacked a specific endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle. The third party's right to recover from the insurer is statutory and paramount.
supporting.fact_alignment: The case involved a commercial vehicle (Maxi Cab) where the driver held an LMV licence but no commercial endorsement. Our case involves a commercial truck where the driver held no valid licence at all. The principle that third-party rights override policy conditions applies a fortiori.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Supreme Court judgment that directly establishes the primacy of third-party rights over policy breaches. It anchors the argument that National Insurance Co. must pay first and recover later.
supporting.quote: the insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained in the driving licence. In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer's liability to satisfy a third-party award is statutory under Section 149 MV Act. Even if a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence) is proved, the insurer must pay the third party and can recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The case involved a third-party death claim where the driver had an invalid licence. The court held the insurer liable to pay and recover. Directly on point with our facts.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Delhi High Court judgment synthesises the entire line of Supreme Court authority (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the 'pay and recover' principle applies even where the insurer proves a fundamental breach.
supporting.quote: the liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Under Section 149(1) and (4) MV Act, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award as a judgment debtor even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, and is entitled to recover from the insured.
